nameStory: Orpine gets its name from the golden pigment 'orpiment' that was once used in painting, referring to the yellowish tones sometimes found in its flowers. Its many folk names like 'live-forever' and 'life-everlasting' come from the plant's remarkable ability to survive and even bloom after being picked - the thick, water-storing leaves keep it alive for weeks without soil!
description: Orpine is a sturdy succulent perennial that looks more like it belongs in a desert than New England. It grows 1-2 feet tall with thick, fleshy leaves that feel rubbery to the touch and store water like a cactus. In late summer, it produces dense, flat-topped clusters of small star-shaped flowers that can range from deep pink to reddish-purple, or sometimes creamy white. The whole plant has a robust, architectural look that makes it stand out among other wildflowers.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, fleshy, oval leaves that feel like rubber erasers when squeezed - they're packed with stored water and won't wilt easily even when picked

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, flat-topped clusters of tiny star-shaped flowers, each with 5 petals, blooming in shades of pink, red-purple, or creamy white

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Sturdy, upright stems 1-2 feet tall that feel solid and substantial, unlike the hollow or thin stems of most wildflowers

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry seed capsules that split open in fall, releasing tiny seeds from the dried flower clusters

habitat: Orpine thrives in sunny, well-drained spots like rocky outcrops, stone walls, old foundations, and disturbed soils where other plants struggle. Originally a garden escape, it's now naturalized in parts of New England, especially around old homesteads and along roadsides. It prefers poor, sandy or gravelly soils and can tolerate drought conditions that would stress most other perennials.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as clusters of thick, rubbery leaves from ground level, often with a blue-green or purplish tint.
seasonality.summer: Sturdy flower stems develop through mid-summer, topped with dense buds that open into showy flower clusters by late summer.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade to brown seed heads that persist, while leaves may turn reddish or purple before dying back to ground level.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to ground level, leaving no above-ground traces until spring growth returns.

funFact: If you pick a stem of orpine and hang it upside down, it can actually continue blooming for weeks without water or soil - Victorian people used this trick to create long-lasting 'living bouquets' that seemed almost magical in their persistence!
confusionNotes: The thick, succulent leaves make orpine almost impossible to confuse with any native New England wildflower - most people mistake it for a houseplant that somehow ended up growing outside! If you can pinch the leaves and feel them squish with stored water, you've found orpine.
contextualKnowledge: Orpine is often sold in garden centers under the name 'Autumn Joy' sedum, and many of the plants found growing wild are actually garden escapees. The scientific name recently changed from Sedum to Hylotelephium, so you might see it listed under either name in field guides.
compareHints: Orpine differs from other stonecrops in its much larger size and robust growth habit - while most stonecrops are low, creeping plants, orpine stands tall and upright. Its flower clusters are also much denser and showier than the smaller, more scattered flowers of other stonecrop relatives. The leaves are significantly thicker and more substantial than those of related species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Pink Mongolian stonecrop differs from its New England relatives like orpine and garden stonecrop by its trailing, mat-forming habit and distinctive blue-gray leaves.
Garden stonecrop differs from its close relative orpine by having more distinctly spoon-shaped leaves and typically paler flowers.
Butterfly stonecrop is larger and showier than its relatives, reaching 2 feet tall versus the 6-12 inches of most other stonecrops in New England.
Compared to the common Orpine found throughout New England, Tatarinow's stonecrop is much smaller and more compact, staying under a foot tall versus Orpine's 1-3 foot height.
Great Stonecrop is much larger and more robust than its close relative Orpine, with bigger leaves and flower clusters.
